samples.text:
These days, a lot of people use smartwatches and apps on their mobile phones to check their health and fitness. I believe that this technology has more advantages than disadvantages.

The main advantage is that these devices motivate people to be more active. For example, a smartwatch can count how many steps you walk every day and remind you to move if you sit for a long time. When people see their progress on the screen, they feel happy and they want to do more exercise. Also, many apps help people to control what they eat and how many calories they take. Another advantage is that some smartwatches can check the heart rate and the sleep. If there is something unusual, the user can visit a doctor early before the problem become serious.

On the other hand, there are some disadvantages. Firstly, the information from these devices is not always correct, so people may worry about nothing or they may ignore a real problem. Secondly, some people become too obsess with the numbers. They check their phone all the time and feel stressed if they do not reach their target. Finally, these apps collect a lot of personal information about the users, and the companies can sell this informations to other companies without permission.

In conclusion, smartwatches and health apps have some problems, such as privacy and wrong information. However, they encourage people to live more healthy lifestyle and they can help to find health problems early. Therefore, I think the advantages outweigh the disadvantages, but people should use them careful and not trust them completely.
samples.why: Clear judgement · relevant points on both sides with simple examples, limited development · mechanical linking (Firstly, Secondly, Finally) · adequate vocabulary · several word-form, agreement and countability errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
Wearable devices and smartphone applications that track steps, heart rate, sleep and diet have become part of everyday life for millions of people. Although these tools have certain drawbacks, I believe their advantages are greater.

Admittedly, there are some concerns. The data produced by consumer devices is not always accurate, and users may be falsely reassured or unnecessarily alarmed by the figures they see. Some people also become fixated on hitting daily targets, which can turn exercise from an enjoyable activity into a source of anxiety. Privacy is another issue, since these apps gather highly personal information about users' bodies and habits, and it is not always clear how technology companies store or share it.

Nevertheless, the benefits are more significant. The most important is that health tracking encourages people to take responsibility for their own wellbeing. Simple features, such as a daily step count or a reminder to stand up after an hour of sitting, can gradually change habits, and seeing progress over time is a powerful motivation to keep going. In addition, some devices can warn users about irregular heartbeats or poor sleep patterns, prompting them to seek medical advice before a condition becomes more serious. For people with long-term illnesses such as diabetes, apps can make it much easier to record information and share it with doctors, leading to better management of the condition.

Moreover, most of the disadvantages depend on how the technology is used. If people treat the data as a general guide rather than a medical diagnosis, and if governments introduces clear rules on data protection, the risks can be greatly reduced.

In conclusion, although health-monitoring technology raises questions about accuracy, obsession and privacy, its ability to motivate healthier lifestyles and detect potential problems early means that the advantages clearly outweigh the disadvantages.
samples.why: Clear position throughout · both sides extended, with drawbacks conceded then outweighed · logical progression and clear paragraph topics · good collocation (falsely reassured, long-term illnesses) · mostly error-free, one agreement slip.

samples.text:
The use of smartwatches and mobile applications to record everything from daily steps to sleep quality and heart rhythm has become commonplace. While this constant self-monitoring has its downsides, I would argue that, for most users, the advantages outweigh them.

The chief benefit is behavioural. Many people know in principle that they should move more, sleep better and eat more sensibly, but struggle to translate that knowledge into action. By turning vague intentions into concrete, measurable goals and providing immediate feedback, fitness trackers make healthy behaviour visible and rewarding, and features such as streaks or friendly competitions can sustain motivation over months. Beyond motivation, some devices can flag potentially significant irregularities, such as an unusually high resting heart rate, prompting users to consult a doctor sooner than they otherwise would. For people managing chronic conditions, digital records can also give doctors a far richer picture than occasional clinic visits allow.

There are, however, legitimate reservations. Consumer devices are not medical instruments, and inaccurate readings can either create needless anxiety or offer false reassurance. For some individuals, the constant stream of data fosters an unhealthy preoccupation with numbers, turning exercise and even sleep into sources of pressure. Most troubling, perhaps, is the question of privacy: health data is extraordinarily sensitive, and users often have little understanding of how it may be stored, analysed or shared with third parties such as advertisers or insurers.

These concerns warrant stronger regulation and greater user awareness, but they do not negate the value of the technology. Treated as a guide rather than a diagnosis, and protected by robust data laws, health trackers can play a genuinely positive role.

In conclusion, despite issues of accuracy, obsession and data security, the capacity of smartwatches and apps to encourage healthier habits and support earlier medical attention means that their advantages outweigh their disadvantages.
samples.why: Clear, well-justified judgement · ideas extended with precise, relevant support · logical sequencing and skilful cohesion · wide, natural vocabulary (preoccupation, negate, third parties) · wide range of error-free structures.
